25	  are easy to under-size for hover).
26	
27	Never draw a border around a mark to separate it. The gap and the ring are the
28	mechanism; a stroke adds data-weight ink that isn't data.
29	
30	## Labels & legend
31	
32	A **legend is always present for two or more series** — the dependable identity
33	channel; never make the reader rely on color-matching alone. Direct labels then ride
34	the marks to *supplement* it. **A single series needs no legend box**: there is only
35	one color, so the chart's title or subtitle already says what is plotted. A box with
36	one swatch restates the title and costs space.
37	
38	- **Label selectively — never a number on every point.** A value beside every dot or
39	  segment is chaos and goes unread. Label the endpoint, the extreme, or the one series
40	  the story is about; let the axis, the legend, and the tooltip/table carry the rest.
41	  Direct labels work *because* they are sparing — flood the chart and they stop working.
42	- **Direct labels before gridlines; gridlines before a second axis.**
43	- **A label that won't fit doesn't get clipped — measure first.** Only place a label
44	  *inside* a bar or stacked segment when the rendered text fits with comfortable
45	  padding on both sides. If it doesn't fit: for a whole bar/column, move the label
46	  outside the bar end (or to the tooltip if there's no room outside either); for an
47	  *interior* stacked segment (which has no free end),
48	  skip the inline label and let the legend + tooltip carry it. Either way the value
49	  stays in the table view, so nothing is gated. Never use `overflow: hidden` on the
50	  segment to "solve" it — that crops the first/last characters and is worse than no
51	  label. Text never overflows or is clipped by its own mark.
52	- Bars → value at the tip. Columns → value on the cap. Lines → value at the end.
53	- Y-axis ticks: round to clean numbers (0 / 1,000 / 2,000), thousands-comma'd; they
54	  carry the values you didn't directly label, so keep them unless every value is labeled.
55	- **Text never wears the data color.** Marks — bars, lines, dots, area fills — carry
56	  the series color; labels, values, legends, and axis text use **text tokens**
57	  (primary / secondary / muted). A light categorical hue (yellow, aqua) is illegible
58	  as text on the surface. Identity comes from the colored mark *beside* the text — a
59	  dot, a short line-key, a swatch — never from coloring the text itself. A label set
60	  *inside* a colored fill (a stacked segment, a map tile) is the one exception: pick
61	  white or ink by the fill's luminance so it always clears contrast.
62	- **When end-labels collide, don't stack them.** Direct end-labels work when series
63	  separate at the right edge. When lines converge, nudging labels apart vertically
64	  detaches them from their lines and reads as noise — instead use **leader lines**
65	  (a thin connector from label to line-end), facet into **small multiples**, or fall
66	  back to the legend + tooltip. Past ~4 converging series, small multiples is usually right.
67	
68	## Figures — when the form is a number
69	
70	- **Stat tile** contract: `label` (sentence case, no trailing colon) · `value` (Sans
71	  semibold, auto-compact: 1,284 / 12.9K / $4.2M) · `delta` (optional; signed,
72	  vs a named period; color = direction × whether up is good) · `trend` (optional;
73	  12-point sparkline in the de-emphasis hue, current period in the accent).
74	- **Meter:** the fill carries severity (accent → warning → danger); the unfilled
75	  track is a **lighter step of the same ramp** (blue-on-blue, etc.) so state reads
76	  across the whole bar.
77	- **Hero figure.** The single number a dashboard leads with, ≥48px, in the same
78	  sans as everything else (never a display or serif face — it reads as off-brand
79	  decoration). Exactly one per view.
80	- **Proportional figures for big numbers; tabular only in columns.** A large
81	  standalone value (hero figure, stat-tile value) uses the font's default
82	  proportional figures — `tabular-nums` gives every digit the width of a `0`, so a
83	  number like `121` looks loose at display sizes. Reserve
84	  `font-variant-numeric: tabular-nums` for columns of numbers that must align
85	  vertically (table rows, axis ticks).
86	
87	## Texture — the backup channel (opt-in)
88	
89	Where hue fails — full-severity CVD, grayscale print, `forced-colors` — texture
90	carries identity. One directional hand-drawn fill, used at **45° and its 135° mirror
91	only** (never horizontal/vertical — those read as gridlines/bars). Inked tone-on-tone
92	(a step from the fill's own ramp), equal loudness across slots. On value scales the
93	texture is *ordered* (rotation steps with magnitude; arm angle carries the diverging
94	sign) so it never misstates the value. Triggered by an accessibility setting, print,
95	or `forced-colors` — never on by default. (See `palette.md`.)
96

1	# Anti-patterns — what goes wrong
2	
3	Check every chart against this list. If your output matches an entry, it is wrong —
4	fix it before shipping. These are real failure modes, each caught in shipping
5	dashboards.
6	
7	## Color & encoding
8	
9	**❌ Dual-axis charts (two y-scales on one plot).**
10	Why it misleads: the alignment of the two scales is arbitrary, so the chart invents a
11	correlation that isn't in the data. Real example: an "Adoption" chart plotting Users
12	(0–30k) against Sessions (0–800k) — a reviewer flagged it as looking "hallucinated."
13	✅ Do instead: two charts, small multiples, or index both series to a common base
14	(=100 at t0) on **one** axis.
15	
16	**❌ Recolor-on-filter.** Assigning colors by current rank, so filtering out a series
17	repaints the survivors.
18	Why: a reader who learned "Acme is blue" is now misled.
19	✅ Color follows the entity, not its row number. Survivors keep their hue.
20	
21	**❌ Cycling / generating hues past 8.** A 9th categorical color, generated or reused.
22	Why: indistinguishable from an existing slot under CVD; breaks the order check.
23	✅ Fold the tail into "Other," facet into small multiples, or use composite encoding.
24	
25	**❌ Eyeballing colorblind-safety.** "These look different enough."
26	✅ Run `scripts/validate_palette.js`. Adjacent ΔE ≥ 8 (OKLab ×100), or 6–8 WITH secondary encoding.
27	
28	**❌ A value-ramp on nominal categories.** Coloring each bar darker-where-bigger
29	when the categories have no natural order (products, teams, endpoints).
30	Why: it double-encodes bar length as hue, burns the only free channel on
31	information the chart already shows, and fails the categorical checks by design
32	(a ramp spans the lightness band and drops below the chroma floor).
33	✅ One series → one color (slot 1) for every bar. Ordered categories (funnel,
34	tiers, age bands) → the ordinal ramp, validated with `--ordinal`.
35	
36	**❌ Rainbow / non-neighbor sequential.** A multi-hue ramp for magnitude.
37	✅ One hue, light→dark. (Analogous neighbors or semantic heat are the only multi-hue
38	sequential exceptions, always with a scale legend.)
39	
40	**❌ A hue at the diverging midpoint, or two cool hues as the two poles.**
41	Why: the midpoint must read as "nothing"; poles must read as opposite. blue↔aqua
42	fails this (both cool); blue↔red or blue↔orange succeed (warm/cool).
43	✅ Two hues that read as opposite + a neutral gray midpoint.
44	
45	**❌ Status color used for a non-status series** (or a series color used for status).
46	✅ Status tokens only when the color *means* good/bad; categorical when it's identity.
47	
48	## Form
49	
50	**❌ Eight categorical hues when the story is one number.** The most common way a
51	chart misses its point.
52	✅ Emphasis (highlight one, gray the rest), or a stat tile / hero number.
53	
54	**❌ A one-bar bar chart, or a 2-slice pie.**
55	✅ A stat tile. The number is the chart.
56	
57	**❌ A donut/pie for comparing close values.**
58	✅ A bar, or the numbers. Part-to-whole at a glance only, ≤ 6 segments.
59	
60	**❌ More than ~7 color classes carrying meaning.**
61	✅ A table, or table + chart. Past ~7 bins, adjacent classes blur.
62	
63	## Marks & chrome
64	
65	**❌ Thick saturated blocks, heavy gridlines, no breathing room.** Reads loud, even
66	childish, at scale.
67	✅ Thin marks, hairline recessive grid/axes, generous padding. Saturated fills are
68	for small marks and accents, never large blocks.
69	
70	**❌ Dashed gridlines or axis rules.** Dashing adds visual noise and reads as
71	"projection" or "threshold" when it's just a grid.
72	✅ Gridlines and axes are solid hairlines, one shade off the surface.
73	
74	**❌ A number on every data point.** A value beside every dot or segment is chaos and goes unread.
75	✅ A legend is always present for ≥ 2 series; direct-label *selectively* (the endpoint, the extreme, the one series that matters) and let the axis + tooltip carry the rest.
76	
77	**❌ A border drawn around marks to separate them.**
78	✅ A 2px surface gap between fills (stacked segments and adjacent bars alike) and a 2px surface ring (on overlapping markers).
79	
80	**❌ A label clipped by, or overflowing, a too-small bar or stacked segment** —
81	including `overflow: hidden` cropping the first/last characters of an in-segment label.
82	✅ Only render a label inside a mark when it fits with padding; otherwise move it
83	outside the bar end, or drop it to the tooltip/legend (the value stays in the table view).
84	
85	**❌ A chart container whose fixed height excludes the x-axis band** — the plot
86	fits, the axis labels don't, so the card gets a tiny nested vertical scroll.
87	✅ Size the container to include the axis labels (plot height + x-axis band),
88	or let the container grow with its content instead of fixing a height.
89	
90	**❌ A display or serif face on the hero figure.** It reads as off-brand decoration.
91	✅ The hero figure uses the same sans as everything else.
92	
93	**❌ `tabular-nums` on a large standalone number.** Equal-width digits make `121`
94	look loose at display sizes.
95	✅ Proportional figures on hero and stat-tile values; `tabular-nums` only where
96	numbers align vertically (table rows, axis ticks).
97	
98	**❌ Texture on by default, or as decoration.** Dense angled fields are a vestibular
99	risk and read as noise on value scales.
100	✅ Texture is opt-in (a11y setting, print, forced-colors), 45°/135° only, ordered on
101	value scales.
102	
103	## Interaction & accessibility
104	
105	**❌ A tooltip as the only way to read a value.**
106	✅ Tooltips enhance, never gate — every value is also reachable via direct labels or
107	the table view; keyboard focus shows the same as hover.
108	
109	**❌ Pinpoint hover targets — an 8px scatter dot you must land on dead-center.**
110	✅ The hit area includes the 2px gap and meets a ~24px minimum; dense scatter uses a nearest-point / Voronoi layer.
111	
112	**❌ Per-chart filters, or filters inside a chart card.**
113	✅ One filter row above everything it scopes; all charts re-render against the same slice.
114	
115	**❌ Skeleton flash on refetch.**
116	✅ Hold the previous render at reduced opacity — no layout jump.
117	
118	**❌ No table view / color-only encoding on a continuous scale.**
119	✅ Every chart has a table-view twin (the WCAG-clean equivalent).
120

#!/usr/bin/env python3
"""
build_data.py -- fetch a date range and merge it into the JSON the dashboard reads.

Everything analytical lives in de_trade_balance.py; this only reshapes its output
into one record per day and upserts it into docs/data/daily.json, so a daily cron
and a one-off backfill are the same code path.

    ./build_data.py                          # yesterday, into docs/data/daily.json
    ./build_data.py --date 2026-07           # all of July
    ./build_data.py --date 2026-07-17 --days 31
    ./build_data.py --source entsoe          # gross per-direction flows, needs a token

Upsert is by date, so re-running a day overwrites it in place -- which is what you
want, because both sources revise the last few days after first publication.

Each record carries the source it came from. That matters: balance_at_de_price,
congestion_rent and the whole daily series are net-only and agree across sources
to well under a percent, but the gross columns (import_gwh, export_gwh, the
volume-weighted prices) are ~26% low from energy-charts, which reports flows
already netted. The dashboard says which source it is showing for that reason.
"""

from __future__ import annotations

import argparse
import json
import os
import sys

import pandas as pd

import de_trade_balance as dtb

HERE = os.path.dirname(os.path.abspath(__file__))
OUT = os.path.join(HERE, "docs", "data", "daily.json")
SCHEMA = 1


def _n(v, digits=2):
    """JSON-safe number: NaN/inf become null, everything else rounds."""
    if v is None or not pd.notna(v):
        return None
    return round(float(v), digits)


def day_records(d: pd.DataFrame, source: str, flows: str) -> list[dict]:
    """One record per calendar day, with its per-border breakdown nested."""
    day = dtb.per_period(d, "day")
    per_bd = dtb.per_border_period(d, "day")

    # the day's mean day-ahead price, deduplicated across borders first
    px = dtb._across_borders(d)["price_de"]
    px = px.groupby(dtb.period_of(px.index, "day")).mean()

    out = []
    for date, r in day.iterrows():
        borders = {}
        if date in per_bd.index.get_level_values("day"):
            for border, b in per_bd.xs(date, level="day").iterrows():
                borders[border] = {
                    "import_gwh": _n(b["import_GWh"]),
                    "export_gwh": _n(b["export_GWh"]),
                    "net_import_gwh": _n(b["net_imp_GWh"]),
                    "bal_de_keur": _n(b["bal_de_kEUR"], 1),
                    "rent_keur": _n(b["rent_kEUR"], 1),
                    "mean_spread": _n(b["mean_spread"]),
                }
        out.append({
            "date": date,
            "source": source,
            "flows": flows,
            "price_de_mean": _n(px.get(date)),
            "import_gwh": _n(r["import_GWh"]),
            "export_gwh": _n(r["export_GWh"]),
            "net_import_gwh": _n(r["net_imp_GWh"]),
            "imp_px_de": _n(r["imp_px_de"]),
            "exp_px_de": _n(r["exp_px_de"]),
            "bal_de_keur": _n(r["bal_de_kEUR"], 1),
            "bal_zonal_keur": _n(r["bal_zonal_kEUR"], 1),
            "rent_keur": _n(r["rent_kEUR"], 1),
            "borders": borders,
        })
    return out


def merge(path: str, fresh: list[dict], borders_asked: list) -> dict:
    """Upsert by date into whatever is already on disk."""
    try:
        with open(path) as fh:
            store = json.load(fh)
    except (OSError, ValueError):
        store = {}

    by_date = {r["date"]: r for r in store.get("days", [])}
    added = sum(1 for r in fresh if r["date"] not in by_date)
    by_date.update({r["date"]: r for r in fresh})

    store["schema"] = SCHEMA
    store["generated_at"] = pd.Timestamp.now(tz=dtb.TZ).isoformat(timespec="seconds")
    store["timezone"] = dtb.TZ
    store["borders_requested"] = list(borders_asked)
    store["units"] = {"gwh": "GWh", "keur": "thousand EUR", "px": "EUR/MWh"}
    store["days"] = [by_date[k] for k in sorted(by_date)]
    print(f"  {added} new day(s), {len(fresh) - added} updated, "
          f"{len(store['days'])} total")
    return store


def write(path: str, store: dict) -> None:
    os.makedirs(os.path.dirname(path), exist_ok=True)
    tmp = f"{path}.tmp"
    with open(tmp, "w") as fh:
        json.dump(store, fh, indent=1, sort_keys=False)
        fh.write("\n")
    os.replace(tmp, path)


def main() -> None:
    ap = argparse.ArgumentParser(description=__doc__.split("\n\n")[0],
                                 formatter_class=argparse.RawDescriptionHelpFormatter)
    ap.add_argument("--date", default=(pd.Timestamp.now(tz=dtb.TZ) - pd.Timedelta(days=1))
                    .strftime("%Y-%m-%d"),
                    help="start: YYYY-MM-DD, YYYY-MM or YYYY (default: yesterday)")
    ap.add_argument("--end", help="last day, inclusive; same forms as --date")
    ap.add_argument("--days", type=int, help="length in days instead of --end")
    ap.add_argument("--flows", choices=["scheduled", "physical"], default="scheduled")
    ap.add_argument("--freq", default="60min")
    ap.add_argument("--borders", help="comma-separated subset")
    ap.add_argument("--source", choices=["energy-charts", "entsoe", "demo"],
                    default=os.environ.get("DE_TRADE_SOURCE", "energy-charts"))
    ap.add_argument("--token", default=os.environ.get("ENTSOE_API_TOKEN"))
    ap.add_argument("--out", default=OUT, help=f"JSON store (default: {OUT})")
    ap.add_argument("--no-cache", action="store_true")
    ap.add_argument("--refresh", action="store_true")
    a = ap.parse_args()

    start = pd.Timestamp(a.date, tz=dtb.TZ).normalize()
    end = (pd.Timestamp(a.end, tz=dtb.TZ).normalize() + dtb.span_of(a.end) if a.end
           else start + pd.DateOffset(days=a.days) if a.days
           else start + dtb.span_of(a.date))
    if end <= start:
        sys.exit("Empty range.")
    borders = [b.strip() for b in a.borders.split(",")] if a.borders else dtb.NEIGHBOURS

    cache = None if (a.no_cache or a.source != "energy-charts") else dtb.Cache(
        dtb.default_cache_dir(), refresh=a.refresh)
    if a.source == "demo":
        backend = dtb.DemoBackend()
    elif a.source == "entsoe":
        if not a.token:
            sys.exit("Set ENTSOE_API_TOKEN or pass --token.")
        backend = dtb.EntsoeBackend(a.token)
    else:
        backend = dtb.EnergyChartsBackend(cache=cache)

    print(f"{start.date()} .. {(end - pd.Timedelta(days=1)).date()} "
          f"via {a.source} ({a.flows})", file=sys.stderr)
    raw = dtb.collect_range(backend, start, end, a.freq, a.flows == "physical",
                            borders, "month")
    d = dtb.value(raw, pd.Timedelta(a.freq) / pd.Timedelta("1h"))
    if cache:
        cache.report()

    write(a.out, merge(a.out, day_records(d, a.source, a.flows), borders))
    print(f"  -> {a.out}")


if __name__ == "__main__":
    main()

Germany's cross-border power balance

What imported electricity cost against what exports earned, valued at German day-ahead prices, day by day.

Balance over the window
—

Daily balance

Export revenue minus import cost, both at the German price.

deficit surplus

Why: bought dear, sold cheap

Volume-weighted German price in the hours Germany imported, against the hours it exported. Both are the same price curve — the gap is timing.

when importing when exporting

Volumes

Energy crossing the border each day.

imported exported

By border

Balance per neighbouring bidding zone, summed over the window.

Table view — every value on this page

Day-ahead prices for Germany and its neighbours are CC BY 4.0 from Bundesnetzagentur | SMARD.de, redistributed by Energy-Charts.info (Fraunhofer ISE), which is also the source of the cross-border exchange series.

Three caveats worth carrying: this is day-ahead only, so intraday and balancing trades are missing; the balance is what the volume was worth at each side's zonal price, not a payment anyone makes, since cross-border trade in the coupled market is implicit; and congestion rent is revenue to the transmission operators on both sides of a border, not a loss.

# gstack browse: QA Testing & Dogfooding

Persistent headless Chromium. First call auto-starts (~3s), then ~100-200ms per command.
Auto-shuts down after 30 min idle. State persists between calls (cookies, tabs, sessions).

## SETUP (run this check BEFORE any browse command)

```bash
_ROOT=$(git rev-parse --show-toplevel 2>/dev/null)
B=""
[ -n "$_ROOT" ] && [ -x "$_ROOT/.claude/skills/gstack/browse/dist/browse" ] && B="$_ROOT/.claude/skills/gstack/browse/dist/browse"
[ -z "$B" ] && B=~/.claude/skills/gstack/browse/dist/browse
if [ -x "$B" ]; then
  echo "READY: $B"
else
  echo "NEEDS_SETUP"
fi
```

If `NEEDS_SETUP`:
1. Tell the user: "gstack browse needs a one-time build (~10 seconds). OK to proceed?" Then STOP and wait.
2. Run: `cd <SKILL_DIR> && ./setup`
3. If `bun` is not installed: `curl -fsSL https://bun.sh/install | bash`

## IMPORTANT

- Use the compiled binary via Bash: `$B <command>`
- NEVER use `mcp__claude-in-chrome__*` tools. They are slow and unreliable.
- Browser persists between calls — cookies, login sessions, and tabs carry over.
- Dialogs (alert/confirm/prompt) are auto-accepted by default — no browser lockup.
- **Show screenshots:** After `$B screenshot`, `$B snapshot -a -o`, or `$B responsive`, always use the Read tool on the output PNG(s) so the user can see them. Without this, screenshots are invisible.

## QA Workflows

### Test a user flow (login, signup, checkout, etc.)

```bash
# 1. Go to the page
$B goto https://app.example.com/login

# 2. See what's interactive
$B snapshot -i

# 3. Fill the form using refs
$B fill @e3 "test@example.com"
$B fill @e4 "password123"
$B click @e5

# 4. Verify it worked
$B snapshot -D              # diff shows what changed after clicking
$B is visible ".dashboard"  # assert the dashboard appeared
$B screenshot /tmp/after-login.png
```

### Verify a deployment / check prod

```bash
$B goto https://yourapp.com
$B text                          # read the page — does it load?
$B console                       # any JS errors?
$B network                       # any failed requests?
$B js "document.title"           # correct title?
$B is visible ".hero-section"    # key elements present?
$B screenshot /tmp/prod-check.png
```

### Dogfood a feature end-to-end

```bash
# Navigate to the feature
$B goto https://app.example.com/new-feature

# Take annotated screenshot — shows every interactive element with labels
$B snapshot -i -a -o /tmp/feature-annotated.png

# Find ALL clickable things (including divs with cursor:pointer)
$B snapshot -C

# Walk through the flow
$B snapshot -i          # baseline
$B click @e3            # interact
$B snapshot -D          # what changed? (unified diff)

# Check element states
$B is visible ".success-toast"
$B is enabled "#next-step-btn"
$B is checked "#agree-checkbox"

# Check console for errors after interactions
$B console
```

### Test responsive layouts

```bash
# Quick: 3 screenshots at mobile/tablet/desktop
$B goto https://yourapp.com
$B responsive /tmp/layout

# Manual: specific viewport
$B viewport 375x812     # iPhone
$B screenshot /tmp/mobile.png
$B viewport 1440x900    # Desktop
$B screenshot /tmp/desktop.png

# Element screenshot (crop to specific element)
$B screenshot "#hero-banner" /tmp/hero.png
$B snapshot -i
$B screenshot @e3 /tmp/button.png

# Region crop
$B screenshot --clip 0,0,800,600 /tmp/above-fold.png

# Viewport only (no scroll)
$B screenshot --viewport /tmp/viewport.png
```

### Test file upload

```bash
$B goto https://app.example.com/upload
$B snapshot -i
$B upload @e3 /path/to/test-file.pdf
$B is visible ".upload-success"
$B screenshot /tmp/upload-result.png
```

### Test forms with validation

```bash
$B goto https://app.example.com/form
$B snapshot -i

# Submit empty — check validation errors appear
$B click @e10                        # submit button
$B snapshot -D                       # diff shows error messages appeared
$B is visible ".error-message"

# Fill and resubmit
$B fill @e3 "valid input"
$B click @e10
$B snapshot -D                       # diff shows errors gone, success state
```

### Test dialogs (delete confirmations, prompts)

```bash
# Set up dialog handling BEFORE triggering
$B dialog-accept              # will auto-accept next alert/confirm
$B click "#delete-button"     # triggers confirmation dialog
$B dialog                     # see what dialog appeared
$B snapshot -D                # verify the item was deleted

# For prompts that need input
$B dialog-accept "my answer"  # accept with text
$B click "#rename-button"     # triggers prompt
```

### Test authenticated pages (import real browser cookies)

```bash
# Import cookies from your real browser (opens interactive picker)
$B cookie-import-browser

# Or import a specific domain directly
$B cookie-import-browser comet --domain .github.com

# Now test authenticated pages
$B goto https://github.com/settings/profile
$B snapshot -i
$B screenshot /tmp/github-profile.png
```

### Compare two pages / environments

```bash
$B diff https://staging.app.com https://prod.app.com
```

### Multi-step chain (efficient for long flows)

```bash
echo '[
  ["goto","https://app.example.com"],
  ["snapshot","-i"],
  ["fill","@e3","test@test.com"],
  ["fill","@e4","password"],
  ["click","@e5"],
  ["snapshot","-D"],
  ["screenshot","/tmp/result.png"]
]' | $B chain
```

## Quick Assertion Patterns

```bash
# Element exists and is visible
$B is visible ".modal"

# Button is enabled/disabled
$B is enabled "#submit-btn"
$B is disabled "#submit-btn"

# Checkbox state
$B is checked "#agree"

# Input is editable
$B is editable "#name-field"

# Element has focus
$B is focused "#search-input"

# Page contains text
$B js "document.body.textContent.includes('Success')"

# Element count
$B js "document.querySelectorAll('.list-item').length"

# Specific attribute value
$B attrs "#logo"    # returns all attributes as JSON

# CSS property
$B css ".button" "background-color"
```

## Snapshot System

The snapshot is your primary tool for understanding and interacting with pages.

```
-i        --interactive           Interactive elements only (buttons, links, inputs) with @e refs
-c        --compact               Compact (no empty structural nodes)
-d <N>    --depth                 Limit tree depth (0 = root only, default: unlimited)
-s <sel>  --selector              Scope to CSS selector
-D        --diff                  Unified diff against previous snapshot (first call stores baseline)
-a        --annotate              Annotated screenshot with red overlay boxes and ref labels
-o <path> --output                Output path for annotated screenshot (default: <temp>/browse-annotated.png)
-C        --cursor-interactive    Cursor-interactive elements (@c refs — divs with pointer, onclick)
```

All flags can be combined freely. `-o` only applies when `-a` is also used.
Example: `$B snapshot -i -a -C -o /tmp/annotated.png`

**Ref numbering:** @e refs are assigned sequentially (@e1, @e2, ...) in tree order.
@c refs from `-C` are numbered separately (@c1, @c2, ...).

After snapshot, use @refs as selectors in any command:
```bash
$B click @e3       $B fill @e4 "value"     $B hover @e1
$B html @e2        $B css @e5 "color"      $B attrs @e6
$B click @c1       # cursor-interactive ref (from -C)
```

**Output format:** indented accessibility tree with @ref IDs, one element per line.
```
  @e1 [heading] "Welcome" [level=1]
  @e2 [textbox] "Email"
  @e3 [button] "Submit"
```

Refs are invalidated on navigation — run `snapshot` again after `goto`.

## Command Reference

### Navigation
| Command | Description |
|---------|-------------|
| `back` | History back |
| `forward` | History forward |
| `goto <url>` | Navigate to URL |
| `reload` | Reload page |
| `url` | Print current URL |

### Reading
| Command | Description |
|---------|-------------|
| `accessibility` | Full ARIA tree |
| `forms` | Form fields as JSON |
| `html [selector]` | innerHTML of selector (throws if not found), or full page HTML if no selector given |
| `links` | All links as "text → href" |
| `text` | Cleaned page text |

### Interaction
| Command | Description |
|---------|-------------|
| `click <sel>` | Click element |
| `cookie <name>=<value>` | Set cookie on current page domain |
| `cookie-import <json>` | Import cookies from JSON file |
| `cookie-import-browser [browser] [--domain d]` | Import cookies from installed Chromium browsers (opens picker, or use --domain for direct import) |
| `dialog-accept [text]` | Auto-accept next alert/confirm/prompt. Optional text is sent as the prompt response |
| `dialog-dismiss` | Auto-dismiss next dialog |
| `fill <sel> <val>` | Fill input |
| `header <name>:<value>` | Set custom request header (colon-separated, sensitive values auto-redacted) |
| `hover <sel>` | Hover element |
| `press <key>` | Press key — Enter, Tab, Escape, ArrowUp/Down/Left/Right, Backspace, Delete, Home, End, PageUp, PageDown, or modifiers like Shift+Enter |
| `scroll [sel]` | Scroll element into view, or scroll to page bottom if no selector |
| `select <sel> <val>` | Select dropdown option by value, label, or visible text |
| `type <text>` | Type into focused element |
| `upload <sel> <file> [file2...]` | Upload file(s) |
| `useragent <string>` | Set user agent |
| `viewport <WxH>` | Set viewport size |
| `wait <sel|--networkidle|--load>` | Wait for element, network idle, or page load (timeout: 15s) |

### Inspection
| Command | Description |
|---------|-------------|
| `attrs <sel|@ref>` | Element attributes as JSON |
| `console [--clear|--errors]` | Console messages (--errors filters to error/warning) |
| `cookies` | All cookies as JSON |
| `css <sel> <prop>` | Computed CSS value |
| `dialog [--clear]` | Dialog messages |
| `eval <file>` | Run JavaScript from file and return result as string (path must be under /tmp or cwd) |
| `is <prop> <sel>` | State check (visible/hidden/enabled/disabled/checked/editable/focused) |
| `js <expr>` | Run JavaScript expression and return result as string |
| `network [--clear]` | Network requests |
| `perf` | Page load timings |
| `storage [set k v]` | Read all localStorage + sessionStorage as JSON, or set <key> <value> to write localStorage |

### Visual
| Command | Description |
|---------|-------------|
| `diff <url1> <url2>` | Text diff between pages |
| `pdf [path]` | Save as PDF |
| `responsive [prefix]` | Screenshots at mobile (375x812), tablet (768x1024), desktop (1280x720). Saves as {prefix}-mobile.png etc. |
| `screenshot [--viewport] [--clip x,y,w,h] [selector|@ref] [path]` | Save screenshot (supports element crop via CSS/@ref, --clip region, --viewport) |

### Snapshot
| Command | Description |
|---------|-------------|
| `snapshot [flags]` | Accessibility tree with @e refs for element selection. Flags: -i interactive only, -c compact, -d N depth limit, -s sel scope, -D diff vs previous, -a annotated screenshot, -o path output, -C cursor-interactive @c refs |

### Meta
| Command | Description |
|---------|-------------|
| `chain` | Run commands from JSON stdin. Format: [["cmd","arg1",...],...] |

### Tabs
| Command | Description |
|---------|-------------|
| `closetab [id]` | Close tab |
| `newtab [url]` | Open new tab |
| `tab <id>` | Switch to tab |
| `tabs` | List open tabs |

### Server
| Command | Description |
|---------|-------------|
| `handoff [message]` | Open visible Chrome at current page for user takeover |
| `restart` | Restart server |
| `resume` | Re-snapshot after user takeover, return control to AI |
| `status` | Health check |
| `stop` | Shutdown server |

## Tips

1. **Navigate once, query many times.** `goto` loads the page; then `text`, `js`, `screenshot` all hit the loaded page instantly.
2. **Use `snapshot -i` first.** See all interactive elements, then click/fill by ref. No CSS selector guessing.
3. **Use `snapshot -D` to verify.** Baseline → action → diff. See exactly what changed.
4. **Use `is` for assertions.** `is visible .modal` is faster and more reliable than parsing page text.
5. **Use `snapshot -a` for evidence.** Annotated screenshots are great for bug reports.
6. **Use `snapshot -C` for tricky UIs.** Finds clickable divs that the accessibility tree misses.
7. **Check `console` after actions.** Catch JS errors that don't surface visually.
8. **Use `chain` for long flows.** Single command, no per-step CLI overhead.

input.content:
name: Daily balance

# Refreshes docs/data/daily.json and commits it. Pages serves docs/ straight from
# the branch, so the commit *is* the deploy -- there is nothing to publish here.
#
# Two things to know about the schedule:
#   * GitHub only fires `schedule` on the repository's DEFAULT branch. While this
#     lives on a side branch, the cron never runs; use workflow_dispatch, or make
#     this the default branch / merge it.
#   * It re-fetches the last few days rather than only yesterday, because both
#     sources revise recent days after first publication. Upsert is by date, so
#     re-fetching corrects a day in place instead of duplicating it.

on:
  schedule:
    - cron: "0 6 * * *"        # 06:00 UTC, comfortably after D-1 is settled
  workflow_dispatch:
    inputs:
      date:
        description: "Start: YYYY-MM-DD, YYYY-MM or YYYY (blank = last 3 days)"
        required: false
      end:
        description: "End, inclusive (optional)"
        required: false

permissions:
  contents: write

concurrency:
  group: daily-balance         # never let two runs race on the same file
  cancel-in-progress: false

jobs:
  build:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4

      - uses: actions/setup-python@v5
        with:
          python-version: "3.12"

      - run: pip install --quiet pandas requests

      - name: Fetch and merge
        # Inputs arrive as env vars, never interpolated into the script body --
        # `${{ inputs.date }}` inline would be a shell-injection hole.
        env:
          IN_DATE: ${{ inputs.date }}
          IN_END: ${{ inputs.end }}
        run: |
          set -euo pipefail
          if [ -n "$IN_DATE" ]; then
            if [ -n "$IN_END" ]; then
              python3 build_data.py --date "$IN_DATE" --end "$IN_END"
            else
              python3 build_data.py --date "$IN_DATE"
            fi
          else
            python3 build_data.py \
              --date "$(date -u -d '3 days ago' +%F)" \
              --end  "$(date -u -d 'yesterday' +%F)"
          fi

      - name: Commit if the data moved
        run: |
          set -euo pipefail
          git config user.name  "github-actions[bot]"
          git config user.email "41898282+github-actions[bot]@users.noreply.github.com"
          git add docs/data/daily.json
          if git diff --staged --quiet; then
            echo "no change"
          else
            git commit -m "data: refresh through $(date -u +%F)"
            git push
          fi

# German cross-border electricity balance

Did Germany pay more for imported electricity than it earned from exports? This
values every cross-border flow at day-ahead prices, per border and per market
time unit, and reports it over a day or a range.

```
de_trade_balance.py    the analysis and CLI report
build_data.py          reshapes a range into docs/data/daily.json
docs/                  the dashboard GitHub Pages serves
```

## Quick start

```bash
pip install pandas requests           # entsoe-py too, for --source entsoe
./de_trade_balance.py --date 2026-08-16          # one day, per MTU
./de_trade_balance.py --date 2026-07             # all of July, per day
./de_trade_balance.py --date 2026 --by week      # the year, per ISO week
./de_trade_balance.py --demo                     # synthetic, no network
```

No account needed: it defaults to Fraunhofer ISE's energy-charts API. Every raw
response is cached under `~/.cache/de_trade_balance`, which matters because that
API is rate limited per IP and endpoint and has no bulk export — a cold month of
all 11 borders costs ~90s and about a dozen requests, then it is free forever.

## The dashboard

```bash
python3 build_data.py --date 2026-07-18 --days 30   # fill the data file
cd docs && python3 -m http.server 8731              # then open localhost:8731
```

`build_data.py` upserts by date, so re-running a day corrects it in place. Both
sources revise the last few days after first publication, which is why the daily
job re-fetches a short trailing window rather than only yesterday.

### Publishing it

Settings → Pages → Source: **Deploy from a branch**, branch `site-daily-dashboard`,
folder **`/docs`**. The data file is committed, so each data commit is a deploy;
there is no build step and no CDN — the page is one HTML file with inline SVG
charts and no dependencies.

`.github/workflows/daily.yml` refreshes the data every morning and commits it.
**GitHub only fires `schedule` on the default branch**, so while this sits on a
side branch the cron will not run — trigger it by hand from the Actions tab
(`workflow_dispatch`, optionally with a date range to backfill), or merge this
branch to make the cron live.

## Which source to use

The default needs no auth and is right for the headline numbers. Use
`--source entsoe` (free token in `ENTSOE_API_TOKEN`, plus `pip install entsoe-py`)
when you need gross volumes.

Measured over July 2026, the two agree on `balance_at_de_price` to **0.0002%** and
on `congestion_rent` to 0.6% — not luck, but because both reduce to net-only
expressions per MTU:

```
balance_at_de_price = sum(net_MWh * price_de)
congestion_rent     = sum(net_MWh * spread)
```

so a source that reports flows already netted cannot shift either. What it does
shift is everything gross: energy-charts nets opposite flows within a border-hour,
so `import_gwh`/`export_gwh` come out ~26% low, and the volume-weighted prices are
biased apart. It also does not carry DK_2 — though the Kontek energy is still
there, filed under DK_1, so only the zonal pricing suffers.

## Reading the numbers

There is no single true figure, so three are reported. Cross-border trade in the
coupled day-ahead market is *implicit*: nobody buys a labelled MWh from France.
German buyers pay the German price, the seller abroad receives theirs, and the
difference is congestion rent collected by the transmission operators on both
sides — regulated back into grid fees and interconnector investment, not a loss.

Day-ahead only: intraday and balancing trades settle at other prices and are not
included. The long-form version of all of this is the docstring at the top of
`de_trade_balance.py`.

## Attribution

Day-ahead prices for Germany and its neighbours are
[CC BY 4.0](https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0/) from
[Bundesnetzagentur | SMARD.de](https://www.smard.de), redistributed unchanged by
[Energy-Charts.info](https://www.energy-charts.info) (Fraunhofer ISE), which is
also the source of the cross-border exchange series. Other bidding zones on that
endpoint are marked private/internal use only — don't widen the border list and
then publish the numbers.

content.text:
Built and committed on `site-daily-dashboard` (`40d97f1`).

**Layout.** One column of cards, hero-first, with a single range filter (7/30/90/All) scoping everything below it:

- **Hero** `−€265.3M` over the window, plus five tiles: net import, price when importing, price when exporting, days in deficit, congestion rent
- **Daily balance** — diverging columns off a zero line, with only the extreme direct-labelled
- **Why: bought dear, sold cheap** — the two volume-weighted price curves with the gap washed in; this is the chart that explains the headline
- **Volumes** — imports above the axis, exports below, so direction is encoded by position *and* colour
- **By border** — horizontal diverging bars, window totals
- **Table view** — every value, collapsed by default

One colour language throughout: **red = money out, blue = money in**. Those are the two poles of a diverging pair rather than an arbitrary pick, and I ran the validator instead of eyeballing it — worst-pair CVD ΔE 21.6 light / 19.2 dark against a target of 8, contrast and lightness passing on both surfaces. Dark mode is stepped for the dark surface, not flipped from light.

**Data flow.** `build_data.py` reshapes a range into `docs/data/daily.json` (30 days = 49 KB), one record per day with per-border figures nested. Upsert by date, which the daily job depends on: it re-fetches a 3-day trailing window because both sources revise recent days, and re-running corrects in place. I verified that's idempotent — 30 days stayed 30, dates unique.

**Automation.** `.github/workflows/daily.yml` at 06:00 UTC commits the data file; Pages serves `docs/` from the branch, so the data commit *is* the deploy — no build, no CDN, no dependencies in the page.

Two things you need to know:

- **The cron won't fire yet.** GitHub only triggers `schedule` on the *default* branch. Until this merges to `main`, use the Actions tab (`workflow_dispatch`, which takes an optional date range for backfilling). Documented in both the workflow and the README.
- **You must enable Pages by hand:** Settings → Pages → Deploy from a branch → `site-daily-dashboard` → `/docs`. I can't set that.

**I rendered it and looked at it**, which caught four things the palette validator can't see: date labels colliding at the right edge (`15 Aug16 Aug`), the extreme's value label landing on top of `31 Jul`, the longest border bar's label covering the `DK1` row name, and — at 390px — eight date labels crowding into each other, now derived from plot width instead of a constant. Also fixed a stale tooltip surviving a range change. Final state verified in both themes at 1280px and 390px: no console errors, no horizontal overflow, filters/tooltips/toggle all working.

Worth noting what the data says, since the layout ended up making it obvious: **3,850 GWh in, 3,832 GWh out — just 18 GWh net over 30 days, yet −€265M.** Germany's trade was almost perfectly balanced by volume; essentially the entire deficit is the price gap between the hours it imported (€146.5) and the hours it exported (€77.9). That's the same timing-dominates finding from the July cross-check, now visible at a glance.

It's up: **http://localhost:8731** — open that in your browser.

```bash
# stop it when done
kill 80605      # or: pkill -f "http.server 8731"

# start it again later
cd docs && python3 -m http.server 8731
```

**One gotcha:** you must serve it over HTTP — opening `docs/index.html` as a `file://` URL will show the "No data to show" box. The page does `fetch("data/daily.json")`, and browsers block that from a file origin. Nothing wrong with your setup if you see that; just use the server.

**To change what it shows**, rebuild the data and refresh the page (no build step, the page just re-fetches):

```bash
python3 build_data.py --date 2026-08-01 --days 16     # add/refresh specific days
python3 build_data.py --date 2026-05 --end 2026-07    # widen history
```

That second one is nearly free — April through July are already in your cache from our earlier work, so it'll mostly report cache hits rather than hitting the API. It would also light up the **90 days** and **All** buttons, which are currently disabled/limited because only 30 days are on file. Worth doing if you want to see how the ISO-week-scale ranges look.

**To test the daily job** without GitHub, just run the step it runs:

```bash
python3 build_data.py --date "$(date -u -v-3d +%F)" --end "$(date -u -v-1d +%F)"
git diff --stat docs/data/daily.json
```

(That's the BSD `date` syntax for macOS; the workflow uses GNU `date -d` since it runs on ubuntu-latest.) If you want to exercise the actual workflow YAML including the commit step, that needs [`act`](https://github.com/nektos/act) and Docker — `act workflow_dispatch -W .github/workflows/daily.yml` — but the fetch step above is the part that can actually fail, and the commit step is three git commands.

content.text:
No, it wasn't correct — and the problem was worse than the wording. That paragraph was hardcoded while `source` is recorded *per day*, so it would have been wrong for every source but the default. Fixed in `f44ec76`.

**What it would have claimed for ENTSO-E data:** CC BY 4.0 from Bundesnetzagentur | SMARD.de, redistributed by Fraunhofer ISE — crediting two parties who supplied nothing, while omitting ENTSO-E, whose terms *require* attribution as the source. Both directions of wrong.

**And the case I hadn't considered:** a file built with `--source demo` would have presented invented numbers under a real CC BY licence. That's the worst thing this page could do, so demo data now also raises a banner above the hero:

> **Partly synthetic.** Some days in this window came from the demo backend. Those numbers are invented and must not be quoted.

Attribution is now looked up per source present in the window and concatenated, so a mixed file credits each. The ENTSO-E entry reads:

> Day-ahead prices and cross-border exchange come from the ENTSO-E Transparency Platform, published under Regulation (EU) No 543/2013. Re-use requires attribution to ENTSO-E as the source; much of the platform's data is listed for free re-use under CC BY 4.0, while an individual series can remain the copyright of the reporting TSO — worth checking the platform's terms for whatever you republish.

I verified those terms rather than assuming: ENTSO-E's clause 2.5 publishes a list of data free for re-use without the data owner's prior agreement, with CC BY 4.0 incorporated into that list, and Regulation 543/2013 mandates attribution to ENTSO-E as source. I deliberately hedged on whether our three specific data items sit on the free-re-use list — the platform's own legal pages block scraping (403), so I couldn't confirm item-level coverage, hence "worth checking the platform's terms" and a link, rather than asserting CC BY 4.0 over ENTSO-E data the way the old line did over SMARD's.

**The same signal fixed a second inaccuracy** I'd introduced: the Volumes caveat about gross figures running "roughly a quarter low" is a property of energy-charts' netting, not of the data generally. It now only makes that claim when a netted source is actually in the window, says "gross in each direction" for ENTSO-E, and warns that gross volumes aren't comparable across a mixed range.

One consequence worth flagging: if you switch the daily workflow to `--source entsoe`, days already on file keep their recorded source, so the footer will credit both chains during the transition — correct, but if you'd rather have a clean cut, `python3 build_data.py --date <start> --end <end> --source entsoe --refresh` rewrites those days in place.

content.text:
Now it's unambiguous, and the answer is not what either of us expected. The list has exactly 35 items. Here's what it says about the three series this project uses:

| Series | Article | On the free-re-use list? |
|---|---|---|
| Physical flows | 12.1.g | **Yes** — item #18 |
| Day-ahead prices | 12.1.d | **No** |
| Scheduled commercial exchanges | 12.1.f | **No** |

The entire `12.1.d / e / f` block — day-ahead prices, net positions, scheduled commercial exchanges — is absent. The list jumps from item #17 (`12.1.c`, total capacity already allocated) straight to #18 (`12.1.g`, physical flows). The only "price" items anywhere on it are transmission *capacity* prices (#14), balancing reserve prices (#23), activated balancing energy (#25) and imbalance prices (#27). No wholesale market prices at all. Two independent extractions agree, and the pattern makes sense: market-results data belongs to the power exchanges, not the TSOs.

**So the dashboard as it currently stands is built on two series that CC BY 4.0 does not cover.** Article 2.5 frames the list as data re-usable *without* seeking the primary owner's agreement — which implies data off the list needs it. The exclusion bullets (Moldova, Turkey, some Ukraine items, and the UK interconnectors BritNed/IFA/Nemo Link) are all irrelevant to German borders, but that's moot when the items aren't listed in the first place.

**The irony is sharp: energy-charts was the licence-clean route and we switched away from it.** Its `/price` docs state that DE-LU and every neighbouring zone is CC BY 4.0 from SMARD, "published without changes" — and its blanket API terms put everything else, including `/cbet`, under CC BY 4.0 with attribution to Energy-Charts.info. That's a complete, publishable licence chain for both series. It's also exactly why energy-charts sources prices from SMARD rather than redistributing exchange data, and why its docs warn that other bidding zones are "private and internal use only… direct your inquiries to EPEX SPOT SE."

Two caveats on my finding: this is the **18 October 2023** revision, so a newer one may have added items — worth confirming against the current revision on the legal terms page. And I'm reading a data list, not giving legal advice.

My recommendation: **revert the published dashboard to energy-charts, and keep ENTSO-E for the CLI and private analysis.** You lose nothing on the headline — we measured the balance agreeing to 0.1 kEUR in 265 million — you lose only correct gross volumes and the DK_1/DK_2 split on the public page.

I've left the data as-is pending your call. I'd hold off publishing until then.

content.text:
Read it. It's the Manual of Procedures page — MoP revision packages (v2.1 through v3.5), an overlaps assessment between the Transparency and EB GL regulations, and an implementation roadmap.

**One useful thing for us:** it confirms the article mapping from ENTSO-E's own documentation — **TR Art. 12.1.d = energy prices**. That was the load-bearing assumption in my reading of the re-use list, and it now rests on their document rather than my memory. Combined with the re-use list itself labelling item #18 as "Physical flows → 12.1.g", the two anchors bracket 12.1.f (scheduled commercial exchanges) exactly where I placed it.

**But it says nothing about licensing, re-use terms, or which data items are freely re-usable.** The MoP is about data submission — formats, technical criteria, production-type classification. So it corroborates the mapping without changing the conclusion: day-ahead prices and scheduled commercial exchanges are still absent from the 18 Oct 2023 free-re-use list, and physical flows are still on it.

You cut off my question, and I'd rather not guess at what's behind that. What would you like to clarify? A few things I can imagine being useful:

- **Dig into the MoP zips** — they contain the canonical data-item tables, which would let me cross-check the re-use list's own `#1–35` numbering against article numbers, in case an item covers prices under a description I didn't recognise.
- **Hunt for a newer revision of the re-use list** — mine is nearly three years old, and CC BY 4.0 was added to it by amendment in Feb 2022, so the list does change.
- **Check whether the restriction actually bites for your use** — e.g. if the dashboard stays unlisted/private, or if attribution alone satisfies it in practice, which is a judgement about your risk appetite rather than a fact I can extract from a PDF.
- Or you may have spotted something in the document I read wrongly — in which case tell me and I'll recheck.
what I'm wondering mostly: this is an open data platform by the EU, so why publish data that you then can not use

It isn't a paradox once you separate two things that both got called "publishing" — and our own evidence trail shows the mechanism.

**The mandate is transparency, not licensing.** Regulation (EU) 543/2013 obliges the industry to *expose* this data so market participants can see prices and flows, spot abuse, and trade informed, and so regulators can supervise. That duty is discharged by making it visible and accessible. It says nothing about granting downstream redistribution rights — and publishing something doesn't extinguish rights in it. Those are two separate legal layers stacked on the same numbers.

**ENTSO-E can only license what its members handed it rights to.** It's not an EU body — it's an AISBL, a Belgian non-profit association of transmission operators. Its terms speak of the "Primary Owner of Data," and that owner differs by item:

- Items on the free-re-use list — load forecasts, cross-zonal capacity, allocations, physical flows, redispatch, balancing — are **TSO-owned**. The TSOs collectively agreed to release their own data under CC BY 4.0 (that's the 2019 open-data move, with CC BY 4.0 folded into the list by amendment in 2022).
- The `12.1.d/e/f` block — energy prices, net positions, scheduled commercial exchanges — is **market results**, owned by the power exchanges/NEMOs: EPEX SPOT, Nord Pool and friends. Regulation compels them to feed it to the platform for transparency. It doesn't make them license it for republication — and selling market data is a substantial part of their commercial model.

So the list stops at `12.1.c` and resumes at `12.1.g` precisely along the ownership seam. ENTSO-E couldn't grant CC BY 4.0 over the middle block even if it wanted to.

**We already had independent confirmation of this and didn't recognise it.** energy-charts' own `/price` docs say the non-SMARD zones are "for private and internal use only" and direct licensing enquiries to "the original data providers, including but not limited to **EPEX SPOT SE**." That's the exchange asserting rights over exactly the series ENTSO-E can't sub-license. The list's other exclusions follow the same "who actually agreed" logic rather than anything technical: BritNed, IFA and Nemo Link are UK interconnectors, outside the regulation post-Brexit; Moldova and Turkey are non-EU parties.

**Why the German copy *is* open.** SMARD is run by the Bundesnetzagentur — a public authority, subject to public-sector open-data rules in a way an industry association isn't. It has its own legal basis to publish DE-LU and neighbouring-zone day-ahead prices, and chose CC BY 4.0. Same numbers, different publisher, genuinely different licence. That's why energy-charts can redistribute them "without changes," and why our original stack was licence-clean somewhat by luck.

**One European wrinkle worth knowing:** "it's just numbers, facts aren't copyrightable" is a much weaker argument here than in the US. The EU has a *sui generis* database right protecting substantial investment in compiling a database, so re-utilising a substantial part can be restricted even where no individual figure is. That's the hook that makes this more than a formality on this side of the Atlantic.

**The practical shape of it:** nothing stops you using ENTSO-E data for analysis, however deep — that's what the platform is *for*, and it's why the CLI on ENTSO-E is completely fine. **Redistribution is the constrained act**, and a public dashboard is redistribution. Since SMARD gives you the identical prices under CC BY 4.0, the fix isn't to give up data quality in general — it's to source the *published* page's prices from the publisher that licensed them.

Which is why I'd still revert the dashboard's data to energy-charts and keep ENTSO-E as the CLI default. The cost is confined to the public page's gross volumes and the DK_2 split; the headline balance, congestion rent and daily series are net-only and measured identical to 0.1 kEUR in 265 million. You got it the wrong way round, and I caused the confusion by quoting that warning twice as evidence for the ownership argument without restating who it applies to.

**All 12 zones this project queries are on energy-charts' CC BY 4.0 list** — verified above against the endpoint's own documented list, not from memory. DE-LU plus all 11 neighbours: AT, BE, CH, CZ, DK1, DK2, FR, NL, NO2, PL, SE4. Every one covered.

The "private and internal use only" restriction applies to **the other bidding zones** — ES, NO1, SE1–3, IT-South, GR and so on. Zones we never touch. The list also covers four we don't use (DE-AT-LU, HU, IT-North, SI), so there's headroom before the fence matters.

It's a fence around territory we deliberately stay inside, and `de_trade_balance.py`'s docstring already says exactly this: *"Prices for DE-LU and every zone bordering it are redistributed from SMARD under CC BY 4.0, so this use is fine. Other bidding zones on the same endpoint are marked private/internal use only — don't widen the border list and then publish the numbers."* That warning was written for the case where someone adds ES or NO1 to `NEIGHBOURS` and publishes — which would be a genuine problem.

So the two routes are not symmetrically constrained:

| | prices | cross-border flows |
|---|---|---|
| **energy-charts** | CC BY 4.0 from SMARD, all 12 zones we use, "published without changes" | no per-endpoint notice, so the API's blanket CC BY 4.0 default applies, with credit to Energy-Charts.info |
| **ENTSO-E** | `12.1.d` — **not** on the free-re-use list | `12.1.f` scheduled — **not** on the list; `12.1.g` physical — **is** on it |

The reason they differ is the mechanism from my last message: SMARD is a public authority that licensed these prices openly, so energy-charts gets to pass them along. ENTSO-E holds the same numbers from the exchanges under terms that don't permit onward licensing.

One honest caveat on the energy-charts column: `/cbet` carries no licence sentence of its own, so it rests on the API's general "unless stated otherwise, CC BY 4.0" — an inherited default rather than an explicit grant for that series. That's weaker than the prices, where the grant is spelled out zone by zone. If you want it airtight, a one-line email to Fraunhofer confirming `/cbet` is CC BY 4.0 would close it, and they're the same people who publish the CC BY 4.0 statement for `/price`.

So my recommendation stands and is better-founded than when I made it: revert the published dashboard to energy-charts, keep ENTSO-E for the CLI. Want me to run that?

content.text:
Your second instinct is exactly right, and it's the whole answer: **buying in DK isn't a separate transaction that happens after the auction — it's part of how the price was reached.** Let me build up to that, because the data backs it precisely.

## First, a correction on "highest bidder"

It's *marginal* pricing, not highest-bidder. All supply offers get sorted cheapest-first, demand bids most-expensive-first, and they cross. Everyone who clears pays (or receives) the **same** price — the one set by the last, most expensive offer that was still needed. Bids above the crossing don't clear at all.

So German wind isn't outcompeted by Danish wind. Wind bids near zero and always clears; it just receives whatever the marginal plant set. What imports displace is the **marginal** unit — the last gas or hard-coal plant needed to close the gap.

That reverses the direction of your hypothesis in an important way: **imports don't make the night price high — they make it less high.** At 20:00 the price was €173.7 because solar was gone and demand needed expensive plants. The 8,507 MW flowing in pushed the most expensive German units out of the stack. Without that import the German price would have been *higher*.

## Why there's flow at all, when the market "already cleared"

There is no German auction plus a Danish auction plus trade between them. There is **one** algorithm (SDAC, running EUPHEMIA) clearing every bidding zone simultaneously, with interconnector capacities as constraints, maximising total welfare across the whole coupled area. Prices and flows are computed *together*, in one solve. The flow is an output, not a decision anyone makes afterwards.

Nobody "buys from Denmark." German buyers bid into the German zone and pay the German price. The algorithm has already routed Danish supply in, because doing so raised welfare. So yes — it's part of the same clearing price, precisely as you guessed.

Then why do the zones have *different* prices?

- **Cable has slack** → the algorithm keeps pushing power from cheap to dear until the two prices **equalise**. One price, no rent.
- **Cable saturates** → it can't push more, so prices stay apart. That gap × the flow is the congestion rent.

Our data says the cables bind almost all the time: prices fully converged in only **0–12% of hours** per border (NL best at 12.0%, CH and NO2 at 0.1%). That's why Europe has 11 prices instead of one.

## The profile is textbook

```
hour   price €/MWh    net flow
04         128.5      +5,416 MW  importing
06         141.5      +6,948 MW  importing
14          19.5      -8,816 MW  exporting   ← solar peak
20         173.7      +5,094 MW  importing   ← evening peak
```

Correlation between the German hourly price and net import: **+0.82**. Germany imports when expensive, exports when cheap, and the driver is its own solar profile — the price bottoms at 14:00 (€19.5) and peaks at 21:00 (€174.1).

And the flows follow the spread, as arbitrage requires:

- Imports came from a **cheaper** zone for **73.3%** of imported MWh (9.1% converged, 17.6% dearer)
- Exports went to a **dearer** zone for **81.3%** of exported MWh

The 17.6% "wrong way" isn't market irrationality. Partly it's our known artifacts — unsplit Denmark, netted flows hiding simultaneous two-way movement, hourly averaging over 15-minute clearing, and scheduled exchanges including intraday volume that a day-ahead price doesn't govern. But partly it's genuine: the Core region uses **flow-based** coupling, where capacity is a joint domain across many borders rather than a limit per cable, so an individual border can legitimately carry power "uphill" while the overall solution is optimal.

## The part that matters for reading your own dashboard

This profile is exactly why **the −€265M is not a loss**, and why the headline is the most easily misread number on the page.

Germany imports in expensive hours because that's when it's short — and those imports *lower* the price its consumers pay. It exports in cheap hours because it's long — and those exports earn its generators money that curtailed solar would not have. Every one of those trades improved both sides; that's why the algorithm selected them. Without the interconnectors, German peak prices would be higher and midday solar would be spilled instead of sold.

What the −€265M actually measures is a **valuation asymmetry**: net import correlates with high prices at +0.82, so the same MWh count is worth more coming in than going out. That's a fact about *when* Germany trades, not evidence that anyone extracted value from it. Which is why the timing term dominated (90% of July) while net volume was a rounding error (18 GWh on 5,291).

One nice sighting in the border table: **SE4 shows a persistent +€27/MWh spread with zero flow all month.** If the cable were available, the algorithm would have arbitraged that instantly — you cannot leave €27/MWh on the table in a coupled market. Zero flow against a standing spread means the interconnector was simply out. The mechanism showing itself by its absence.

content.text:
No — and the concept doesn't quite exist in this market design either.

**What we actually get.** `/price` returns exactly this per zone:

```
{"license_info": str, "unix_seconds": [int], "price": [float], "unit": str, "deprecated": bool}
```

One number per market time unit. No technology dimension, and **no bid or order-book endpoint exists on the API at all** — I checked every path for bid/curve/merit/order/offer.

**The deeper reason it can't.** In a uniform-price auction there is no price *per* technology. Everything that clears receives the same price. What differs is:

- what a plant would **bid** — roughly its marginal cost: fuel + CO₂ + variable O&M; near zero, or negative under subsidy, for wind and solar
- what it **receives** — the single clearing price

The gap between those is inframarginal rent, and it's how a wind farm bidding €0 earns €174 at 21:00. So "the price of wind" isn't a published figure; it's the clearing price, same as everyone else's. The only technology-linked price in the system is the **marginal** unit's cost, because that's what sets the clearing price for all of them.

**Where bid-level data does and doesn't live:**

- **Day-ahead aggregated supply/demand curves** — the actual merit-order curves — are published by the exchanges (EPEX SPOT, Nord Pool) for their own markets. Commercially licensed, not on ENTSO-E's platform, not on energy-charts. Exactly the ownership pattern from our licence dig: market microstructure is exchange property.
- **Balancing** bids *are* public: aggregated balancing energy bids sit on ENTSO-E's free-re-use list as item #26 (articles 17.1.d/e/j). So bid-level data exists for balancing, just not for day-ahead energy.
- **Generation per technology** is freely available on both sources — volumes, not prices.

**What you can do with what's licensed** is infer which technology was marginal, by joining the price series to the generation stack. energy-charts' `/public_power` returns 21 series for Germany:

```
lignite · hard coal · fossil gas · fossil oil · coal-derived gas · nuclear-free stack
wind onshore · wind offshore · solar · biomass · waste · geothermal
hydro run-of-river · reservoir · pumped storage (+ its consumption)
load · residual load · renewable share of load / of generation
```

Residual load is the useful one: load minus wind and solar is essentially "how deep into the thermal stack we had to reach," and it tracks price closely. That's how you'd get from our data to "gas set the price at 21:00, solar set it at 14:00" — an inference from volumes plus price, not a lookup.

It would also be **licence-clean**: no per-endpoint restriction on `/public_power`, so it falls under the same blanket CC BY 4.0, and SMARD publishes German generation per type openly too.

Worth adding to the dashboard? It would answer the question your current page raises but can't settle — *what* Germany was importing instead of, hour by hour. A residual-load or stack panel beside the price chart would close that loop. Say the word and I'll scope it.

content.text:
Yes — considerably more detail, and one finding **dissolves the trade-off I told you was unavoidable.**

## The big one: SMARD has gross per-direction cross-border flows

Separate Import *and* Export series per neighbour, with DK1 and DK2 as distinct borders. Cross-validated against ENTSO-E for 18 July:

```
                    SMARD    ENTSO-E   delta
DK_1 into DE       33,349     33,350      -1 MWh
DK_1 out of DE     36,968     36,970      -2
DK_2 into DE       11,939     11,940      -1
DK_2 out of DE      2,503      2,500      +3
```

Identical to rounding. So SMARD gives you **exactly what ENTSO-E gave** — gross volumes, no netting loss, DK_2 as its own border — from a **public authority publishing under CC BY 4.0**. You would not have to choose between correct gross volumes and a publishable licence. That was the whole cost of reverting, and it turns out to be avoidable.

It also puts the `/cbet` soft spot to rest: instead of resting on energy-charts' blanket "unless stated otherwise" default, the flows would carry the same explicit public-authority licence as the prices.

## What else is there

**More than energy-charts:**
- **Prices for 17 zones** — including SE4, Belgium and NO2, which definitively settles that the community `bund.dev` spec I first consulted was just incomplete
- **Installed capacity** per technology
- **Generation forecasts**, day-ahead *and* intraday
- **Residual load**, both realised and forecast — the "how deep into the thermal stack did we reach" series from your last question
- **Balancing energy**: volumes (+/−), **price**, revenues
- **System costs**: balancing expenditure, countertrading, grid-security measures (redispatch)
- **Per-TSO breakdown** — Amprion, TenneT, TransnetBW as separate control areas

**Less than energy-charts, in one respect:** generation is 12 types versus energy-charts' 21. SMARD lumps into "Sonstige Konventionelle"/"Sonstige Erneuerbare" where energy-charts (using ENTSO-E's taxonomy) breaks out fossil oil, coal-derived gas, geothermal, waste, and three hydro categories separately. So for a generation-mix panel, energy-charts is finer; for everything else, SMARD is deeper.

**Still no day-ahead bid curves** — that answers your previous question for SMARD too. `Ausgleichsenergiepreis` is a genuine auction-derived price, but for balancing, not the day-ahead merit order. The day-ahead curves really do stay with the exchanges.

## The API, since it isn't documented anywhere useful

I had to reverse it from the site's own network traffic:

```
manifest   /app/chart_configuration/market_data_configuration.json   (321 modules with IDs)
labels     /app/assets/translations/lang-de.json
regions    /app/chart_configuration/regions.json
download   POST /nip-download-manager/nip/download/market-data → CSV
```

Two gotchas worth recording: the region must be **`DE-LU`** for cross-border modules (`DE` returns "Keine Daten"), and the CSV is German-formatted with imports as **negative** numbers.

## Worth building?

A SMARD backend would give the dashboard ENTSO-E-quality volumes on a licence that permits publishing — strictly better than either source we've used. It's real work: mapping 11 borders × 2 directions to module IDs, German decimal parsing, sign conventions, and a chunking strategy against an undocumented endpoint. Maybe an evening.

Two smaller things it would also unlock: DK_2 finally appearing on the public page, and the residual-load series for the "what set the price" panel we discussed.

Built and committed as `4f77853`. Refresh **http://localhost:8731**.

**SMARD dissolves the trade-off I'd told you was unavoidable.** You now get ENTSO-E's data shape on a licence that permits publishing: gross per-direction flows, DK_2 as a real border, CC BY 4.0 from the primary publisher. Verified against ENTSO-E for 18 July — **all 11 borders, both directions, every one within 0.02 GWh.** The balance moved 0.3 kEUR, being net-only as always.

It's also dramatically cheaper: one POST carries many modules, so a month of every border plus prices and load is **six requests in a couple of seconds**, against ~34 for ENTSO-E and a 90-second rate-limit crawl for energy-charts.

**One bug worth telling you about**, because of how it hid. SMARD returns columns in *its* order, not the order you request modules — but only once a request grows past a handful, which is why my small probes looked fine. Zipping the response to my id list permuted every single border **while leaving the totals exactly correct**. The per-border cross-check against ENTSO-E caught it; a totals check never would have. Columns are now matched by header label, and that's written down in the class.

**The new panel — "What the price had to reach for"** — is a scatter of daily mean price against residual load (demand minus wind and solar), one dot per day, coloured red/blue by whether Germany was a net importer.

A scatter deliberately: those are different measures, and putting GW and €/MWh on a shared time axis would need two y-scales — the one chart form that reliably manufactures a correlation that isn't there. Here each measure owns an axis and the relationship *is* the reading.

It answers what your balance chart structurally cannot: **the price tracks how far into the dispatchable stack the day had to reach (r = 0.79), and the days Germany imported are the days it reached furthest.** Blue dots cluster low-left, red high-right. That's the mechanism from our market-coupling conversation, visible in one panel. Residual load and load also joined the table view and the tooltips.

Verified in both themes at 1280px and 390px, no console errors, no overflow, filters and tooltips exercised. That caught a second bug: the new card was being drawn while still `hidden`, so it measured 0 wide, the fallback width took over, and the SVG scaled down — shrinking every label. Only visible on mobile, where legibility matters most.

Two notes:

- **The daily workflow needs no secret now.** It uses SMARD, no token, and deliberately takes no source input — the licence reasoning is in a comment at the fetch step so nobody switches it casually.
- **`--source entsoe` is now the cross-check**, and it earned that role twice today: it caught the column permutation, and it validated the gross volumes. Worth keeping the token around for exactly that.

You were right that it wasn't working. The chart was *asserting* its finding (an `r = 0.79` in the caption) rather than showing it, and a chart that needs its paragraph to be understood is doing the wrong job. Four changes:

- **The trend line is now drawn** — least-squares, clipped to the plot rectangle so a steep slope can't poke out of the top corner. The relationship is a line you can see instead of a number you have to trust.
- **The x axis says which way it runs**: `← more wind & sun` on the left, `less wind & sun →` on the right. "Residual load" gave you a quantity with no direction to hold in your head; now the axis tells you what moving right *means*.

- **The title states the finding**: "Cheap days are windy days", rather than the riddle "What the price had to reach for". The caption now opens with how to read a single dot.

The read should be, without help: dots climb left to right along the grey line; the left end is blue and cheap, the right end is red and dear. Wind and sun scarce → power dear → Germany imports.

content.text:
Your critique lands, and checking it produced three surprises — including one that inverts your Poland hypothesis.

## Who Germany actually net-imported from, 30 days

| border | net GWh | counterpart price *in the hours it sent to DE* |
|---|---|---|
| **FR** | **+493** | 122.5 |
| **DK_1** | **+460** | 138.1 |
| **NL** | **+310** | 121.2 |
| **NO_2** | **+179** | 139.5 |
| DK_2 | +32 | 122.0 |
| PL | +12 | 121.7 |
| BE | −61 | net *destination* |
| CZ | −90 | net *destination* |
| CH | −408 | net destination |
| AT | −911 | net destination |

**Poland contributed 12 GWh — under 1%.** And Czechia, the other coal-heavy neighbour, was a net *recipient* of 90 GWh from Germany. So on net Germany wasn't importing coal from the east; it was mildly exporting into it.

**France, though, you called correctly**: 493 GWh, the single largest net source, roughly a third of the inflow. Nuclear-heavy. So "we imported wind" is not the honest summary — "France and Denmark, in that order" is.

## The reframe I hadn't seen

Net inflow ~1,486 GWh from north and west; net outflow ~1,469 GWh to south and east. **Netting to 18 GWh.** Germany is functioning as a **corridor** — Nordic wind and hydro plus French nuclear moving through to Austria (911 GWh) and Switzerland (408 GWh). The dashboard's "By border" panel contains this but never says it, and "Germany needs imports" is the wrong reading of it.

## Where your scepticism bites hardest

Look at that last column. Denmark's price averaged **€138 in the hours it exported to Germany, against €112 across all its hours**. NO2: €139.5 versus €116. If Germany were mopping up surplus Nordic wind you'd see €20–40 there. Instead, imports arrive when the *neighbours* are also tight — because Germany imports at peak, and peak is peak everywhere in a coupled system. So "cheap imported wind" isn't what the prices say.

## Your coal-inflexibility point is confirmed in the data

The price bands, with residual load and net flow:

| German price | mean residual load | mean net flow |
|---|---|---|
| negative (61 h, 8.5%) | **−4.3 GW** | −9,195 MW (exporting) |
| €0–20 | −0.7 GW | −8,188 MW |
| €20–60 | +2.1 GW | −6,857 MW |
| €60–120 | +10.9 GW | −3,506 MW |
| over €120 (61.5%) | +31.8 GW | **+4,062 MW** (importing) |

Monotonic across all five bands — the entire mechanism in one table. And the top row is exactly your argument: **residual load goes negative** (wind and solar exceeding *all* demand), price goes to −€12.28, and Germany dumps 9 GW abroad. Something inflexible keeps running rather than shutting — must-run coal and CHP — so the price goes negative instead of the plant going offline. 61 hours of it in a month.

## What this means for the framing

Strictly, no traded MWh carries a technology. The flow is the optimiser's output, so "we imported wind" can never be literally true. What survives is:

- **The German-side claim holds.** High residual load → high price → imports. That's what the two panels show and it's solid.
- **The source claim does not.** The page currently implies renewables scarcity is met by "gas, coal and imports" without saying whose. I should tighten that.

**What would genuinely settle it:** energy-charts publishes `/public_power` per country, so I can pull the exporting zone's generation mix hour by hour and say "when Denmark sent power to Germany, Denmark was 62% wind." Licence-wise that's the blanket CC BY 4.0 with no per-endpoint restriction, so it's publishable. One honest caveat even then: a zone being 62% wind doesn't make wind the *marginal* unit — the price is what reveals the margin, and €138 says it wasn't wind.

Two things I'd build, in order:

1. **A "where it came from" panel** — net flow per border with the counterpart's price, making the corridor pattern and the France/Denmark ranking visible. Cheap; the data is already in the file.
2. **Exporting-zone generation mix**, which is the real answer to your question and needs a new fetch path.

And regardless of both, I'd add that price-band ladder somewhere — it's the clearest thing we've produced all session. Which do you want?
